text: Hey, everybody, in this video I want to talk  about another way that the logic of divine
images comes through in the Hebrew Bible, but  this time I want to talk about how it structures
the Hebrew Bible's discussion of the  messenger of YHWH, the angel of the Lord.
And this figure shows up in a number of  places, and in its earliest occurrences it
actually shows up in narratives where it seems to  be conflated with God themselves. In other words,
we have some narratives where the text will  say in one verse that it is the messenger of
YHWH speaking, and then in the next verse will say  it's YHWH themselves speaking. There are a handful
of verses where this happens, most notably  Genesis 16 with Hagar, Exodus 3 with Moses,
Judges 6 with Gideon, Judges 13 with Manoah  and his wife—those are Sampson's parents.
And there are some interesting features of  these stories. Exodus 3 is a good example.   Verse 2 says that the messenger of YHWH  appeared to Moses in the burning bush.
The rest of the chapter has Moses speaking  directly with God. In fact, this messenger in one
verse says, "I am the God of your fathers, the God  of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob."
And you have another interesting feature where  these people are afraid to look at this entity or
express shock that they have seen this entity and  stayed alive, and this obviously reflects the idea
from Exodus 33:20 that humanity humans can't see  the face of God and live. But there are a number
of considerations to look at here. Before we move  on to how divine image logic is related to this,
where does this messenger come from? Well, I would  argue that it comes from textual interpolation;
that these stories all originated in narratives  about God themselves visiting, interacting with,
speaking with humanity, and at some point this  became theologically problematic, and so a scribe
came in and wrote the word מלאך in front of  the word אלהים or the word יהוה in order to
obscure the presence of God. And there are a few  pieces of evidence that point in this direction.
First, the fact that we have this inconsistency  in the narrative, as with Exodus 3 where it says   the messenger appeared and then the rest of the  narrative speaks as if it is God themselves there.
Second, the messenger is never doing what  messengers do in the narratives where the
identities seem to be mixed up. They're always  doing what God does. Elsewhere messengers do
what messengers do: pass on messages, things like  that, but in these narratives with the conflated
identities they never do what messengers  do. They only do what God does. Three,
the individuals involved always seem to think  they're speaking directly with God, and one of
the indications of this is the fact that they are  always scared about dying because they are looking
at God. For instance, Moses looks away because he  was afraid to look at God. Manoah tells his wife,
"We will surely die because we have seen god."  Hagar says, "Have I really seen God and lived?
And there is—Exodus 33:20 says you cannot  see God's face and live. Nowhere is there
a prohibition on seeing an angel. In fact,  it would entirely undermine the entire point
of using this intermediary messenger figure if  even seeing the messenger figure was deadly.
Because that's what they're there for: to pass  along messages because humanity cannot directly   engage with deity, at least according  to the ideology expressed in Exodus 33.
And then, a couple more considerations. We  know that it was common in the ancient world
for scribes to use the word "angel" to obscure  the presence of God in theologically problematic
activities. For instance, the Septuagint  and the Targumim add an angel in Exodus
4:24. This is the verse about God confronting  Moses and wanting to kill him. Well
in the Septuagint and the Targumim it's an angel  of God, or an angel of YHWH, that confronts Moses.
The Targumim do this quite a bit—add in angels,  including like Jacob's wrestle where he says,
where he names the place Penuel,  "Because I have seen the face of God,"   say, "I've seen face of angels." And we also have  the Samaritan Pentateuch—a number of places where
the מלאך is interpolated in order to obscure  the presence of God. So it was a common practice
anciently for scribes, and finally, there is  textual instability in a lot of the witnesses.
For instance, Exodus 3 verse 2 is the only place  in the whole text where the messenger is mentioned
at all, but the Vulgate doesn't have it. Where  did that come from? Did the Vulgate's source texts
only have God themselves talking with  Moses? There's no messenger in there.   In other—again in the Septuagint and Targumim  and some other ancient versions, the places where
the angel does and does not show up in those  narratives gets mixed, so it's not consistent.
All these lines of evidence converge, I would  suggest, to indicate that the messenger of YHWH is
the product of textual interpolation,  that there was no such title anciently,
but that the need to obscure the presence of  God in theologically problematic activities
produced this addition of the word  צלאך to the text which produced
מלאך יהוה, angel of YHWH, or מאלך אלהים, angel of  God, and this tradition then grew from there. And
so we have some of the later traditions where  the מאלה יהוה is explicitly described in the
third person by God as an angel, and there's  one interesting place where this happens that I
argue is actually an attempt on the part of  the author to make sense of how it can be
that the messenger's identity seems to be  tied into the identity of God, and that's
Exodus 23:20–21, where God says, "I'm sending  my messenger before you to guard you on the way
do not disobey him, don't annoy him, because  he does not have to forgive your sins."
And this is supposed to be something that only  God can do—forgive sins. We know this from—the   New Testament, for instance, makes a big deal  out of this in Mark 2: "Who can forgive sins
but God alone?" And this is most likely  an allusion precisely to Exodus 23:20–21,   because why can the messenger—why does  the messenger have the prerogative,
the authority to forgive sins or not forgive  sins? That's the final clause in the verse:
"for my name is in him." And what this reflects is  the divine image logic, because the divine image
is enlivened, is endowed with the divine agency  because of some kind of ritual. There are a couple
of things that need to take place: the image  needs to be created from appropriate material
and the image needs to go through some  kind of endowment or consecration procedure
whereby the agency is installed in the  image. The imposition of the divine name
could be part of that, and could be a central part  of it, because names anciently were very powerful
vehicles for agency. To know the name of a  deity was to be able to have power. The name
in the afterlife was was one of the guarantees  of continued survival—a successful afterlife.
And the name of authority was used to not just  mark things as under the control of authority,
but to actually reify that authority. And we see  the same thing today in the fact that things that
are signed by significant figures take on  additional value in the eyes of the public,
because that name somehow endows that's—that  object, whatever it is being signed, with
additional significance and this is a more modern  iteration of this sense that names carry power.
And so in the Deuteronomistic literature you  have the temple in Jerusalem identified as the
place where God will place their name. The  idea probably being, the divine image will
bear an inscribed divine name, and that is one  of the things that will localize the deity's
presence in the divine image within the temple.  And so, to say that the messenger has God's name
in him is to say that they carry that  vehicle for divine agency and therefore
exercise God's power, God's authority, and can  even bear God's titles. So this is the way to say,
"Remember all those passages where the angel, the  messenger says, 'I am the God of your fathers'?
Well, it's because they possessed the divine name.  They had the prerogative to invoke those names."
And so this was happening after the conflation,  or at the same time of the conflation,
but early enough that it still appears in our  biblical texts. And this tradition pops up more
in the Greco-Roman Period as we have a number  of other figures that that show up on the scene,   particularly named angels—for instance, the  Apocalypse of Abraham, you have this angel
Yahoel—which is a combination of the word  el, God, and the Tetragrammaton, YHWH—and
that angel therefore has the divine name in their  own name and says that they exercise God's power
in virtue of the divine name which indwells  the messenger, the angel. The Son of Man,
from Daniel 7:13. This becomes a title in the  Greek literature, likely because of the change
of the preposition ἕως in the clause, "The Son of  Man—one like a son of man came to the Ancient of
Days," was changed to ὡς, "the Son of Man came  *as* the Ancient of Days." So we're conflating
identities again, and then we have the Enochic  and other literature that expounds on how this
mediator figure—this messianic mediator figure  who is somehow identified with God because of
the intervention of the divine name, which is  the power to create the earth, for instance,
in some Enochic literature. And so, the messenger  of YHWH starting off as textual interpolation
becomes rationalized as an authorized possessor of  the divine name, just like a divine image would,
and that gets expanded in Greco-Roman Period  literature and you have a number of different
figures who ostensibly um bear that name. And  I would suggest that the early tradition of
Jesus—which consolidates some of these figures,  Son of God, Son of Man, Messiah, prophet, priest,
king, all these things—consolidates  all of these different traditions   within the figure of Christ, and the divine name  is central to the New Testament's presentation
of Jesus identity with God as well. Now, there  are different frameworks for, for deploying it.
Mark has a somewhat adoptionistic framework. John  deploys a logos theology very similar to Philos.
But the divine name is is central to this,  particularly in John, where the "I am" rhetoric
is so systematized. And "I am" in Greek is ἐγὼ  εἰμί, which is the translation of two different
methods of self-identification by YHWH in the  Hebrew Bible: Exodus 3:14: אהיה אשׁר אהיה,
"I will be what I will be," is translated  into Greek as ἐγὼ εἰμι ὁ ὤν, literally,
"I am the one who is," or "the being one,"  but ἐγὼ εἰμί becomes a reference to that,
and ἐγὼ εἰμί is also the translation of the  hebrew אני הוא from Deuteronomy and Isaiah.
"I am he" is also translated as ἐγὼ εἰμί, and  so Christ multiple times in the gospel of John
finds ways to work in the phrase ἐγὼ εἰμί, and  this is not an assertion of identity as God so
much as is it is an assertion of possession  of the divine name, the Tetragrammaton,
"I am," and that indicates to the listeners, "I  am an authorized possessor of the divine name,
therefore I exercise God's power and authority."  And so in Mark 2, when he says the Son of Man has
power on earth to forgive sins, I would suggest  this is a reference back to Exodus 23:20–21. How
could the messenger of YHWH forgives sins? Because  of the indwelling of the name. How can the Son of
Man forgive sins? Same thing. And so the—and  then we have the the hymn in Pphilippians 2,
where Christ has been highly exalted  because Christ is given the name,
and that would be the Tetragrammaton, the divine  name. Now, once we get through the New Testament
into the second century, then we have the rise of  christian apologists who are bringing a lot more
heavy philosophical frameworks to bear on the  question in order to intellectualize the gospel,
to make it more palatable to the Greco-Roman  intelligentsia, and this is where we begin to have
this renegotiation of Christ's identification  with God, and we have the seeds of the Trinity
developing. And so by the fourth century CE  we have this new philosophical framework, the
Trinity, which is basically just a philosophical  rationalization for divine image logic, because
the relationship is the same: we have a separate  entity that in some way identifies with and
as the deity, but is also separate from the  deity. And with divine images that is because
they have been endowed with divine agency  through some kind of vehicle and therefore
manifest the presence of the deity, and this  is precisely what the messenger of YHWH does,   this is precisely what the Son of Man does, and  this is precisely what Jesus does in the New
Testament. And the Trinity is a philosophical—a  different kind of philosophical rationalization
of that logic. So the logic of divine images is  quite critical to many places in the Hebrew Bible
as well as the New Testament and in my next video  I'm going to go back a little bit to the beginning
to talk about the logic of deity—of the  concept of deities—and how that developed
and how our perception of agency in the world  around us sits at the root of deity concepts.
